findings.consequence: A forged cursor with a negative offset used to fail at slicing. It now silently returns the first page. For prev cursors, negative offsets still reach the queryset unchanged.
findings.explanation: The comment in `BasePaginator.get_result` says negative offsets are allowed. The code uses `max(0, offset)` when `not cursor.is_prev`, so a negative offset is clamped to 0 instead of being passed through. The `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check further down still uses the raw `offset`, so it can disagree with `start_offset`. This changes the behaviour of every paginator that inherits from `BasePaginator`.
findings.title: BasePaginator now silently clamps negative offsets for next-direction cursors, and the comment contradicts the code

findings.consequence: The audit-log endpoint returns a 500 for any negative-offset cursor when `optimized_pagination=true` is used. The "negative offset support" the new class advertises does not work. The comments claiming it exposes data "beyond normal pagination bounds" describe unsafe, unvalidated behaviour.
findings.explanation: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, `get_result` takes `start_offset = cursor.offset` and calls `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The comment that the ORM handles negative slicing is wrong. The offset comes from the client-supplied cursor string, which I did not confirm is parsed without a lower bound. The endpoint turns this branch on for any superuser or member with global access who passes `optimized_pagination=true`. Such a user can send a cursor like `0:-5:0` to the audit-log endpoint and trigger the crash. The same branch also sets `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`, so a small negative offset gives a negative or tiny stop. Even if slicing were allowed, the result would not be well defined.
findings.title: Negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start, which Django rejects

prs.title: Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs

findings.consequence: Requests that previously succeeded could return 500 even though they never asked for the optimized path.
findings.explanation: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` runs on every request, including those without optimized_pagination=true. For a non-superuser caller whose organization_context.member is None, such as an API or org-token caller that isn't an org member, this raises AttributeError. Before the change, those callers reached the plain DateTimePaginator path without error. I did not check whether member can be None for this endpoint's permission classes.
findings.title: Admin check is evaluated eagerly and can fail the default path when member is None

findings.consequence: An admin request with optimized_pagination=true and a negative-offset cursor returns a 500 instead of a page. The "optimized" feature cannot work as documented. The claimed ability to read beyond normal pagination bounds is unsupported.
findings.explanation: When enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0, get_result calls queryset[cursor.offset:stop] with a negative start. Django querysets don't support negative indexing, so this raises ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported."). The comment claiming the ORM handles negative slicing is wrong. The cursor offset comes from the client's cursor query parameter. The endpoint passes enable_advanced_features=True whenever optimized_pagination=true and the user is an admin. A cursor such as `0:-5:0` therefore reaches this slice. When stop is also negative or zero the slice is nonsensical as well. The same negative slice is reachable in the else branch for is_prev cursors, and in BasePaginator.get_result, which now passes the raw offset through when cursor.is_prev.
findings.title: Negative-offset path slices a Django queryset with a negative index, which raises instead of paging

findings.consequence: Very deep traces (over 1000 levels) can be flushed as several fragmented segments instead of one. This is an unlikely case, but it is a regression from the previous limit.
findings.explanation: The loop that follows the redirect chain in add-buffer.lua now stops after 1000 hops, down from 10000. The change did not touch redirect-chain resolution, and nothing in the diff explains the lower bound. If a trace has a parent chain deeper than 1000 spans, the loop exits before it reaches the chain's root set. The span is then written to an intermediate set key. The same logic means those deep subtrees are never merged into one segment.
findings.title: Redirect-chain depth limit cut from 10000 to 1000

prs.title: Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert

findings.consequence: Re-installing such an integration into an organization returns an unhandled 500 instead of the intended error page. The user cannot complete the install flow.
findings.explanation: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new ownership check reads integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] directly. The "sender" key is only written in build_integration when the install state contains a sender (see the `integration["metadata"]["sender"] = state["sender"]` line near 377). An existing active Integration with no OrganizationIntegration and no "sender" in its metadata, such as one created before sender was recorded or after its org integration was removed, raises KeyError. The same happens if "sender" is None or has no "login". The check is also unreachable for a not-yet-existing Integration, which skips straight to next_step. I did not read other files to confirm which stored integrations lack the key.
findings.title: Sender check indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] without guarding for a missing key

findings.consequence: After a hang, two flushers handle the same shards: duplicate flushing and producing of segments, and leaked processes that keep accumulating across restarts. On shutdown or rebalance, stuck flusher processes are not terminated.
findings.explanation: The processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` derives from `process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process` (`context.Process`). The new check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is therefore always False for real processes. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally and ignored `ValueError`. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a process flagged "hang" is no longer killed. `_create_process_for_shards` then starts a second process for the same shards while the hung one is still alive. The same isinstance check in `join()` (around line 346) skips `process.terminate()`, so processes that outlive the timeout are never terminated.
findings.title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) never matches spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed

findings.consequence: On shutdown or rebalance with a timeout, some flusher processes can stay alive. They are daemons, so they are only reaped when the parent exits. Until then they keep flushing segments and holding Redis and Kafka resources.
findings.explanation: The old join() always called process.terminate() after waiting. The new per-process loop does `break` when the deadline is exhausted (line 341). Every process after the current one in self.processes is then never waited on or terminated. For example, with 3 flusher processes and a short timeout, if process 0 uses up the budget, processes 1 and 2 are left running.
findings.title: join() skips terminating remaining flusher processes once the deadline expires

prs.title: Span Buffer Multiprocess Enhancement with Health Monitoring

findings.consequence: The `queued` value does not show when the assignment was queued. Any later logic or debugging that relies on it sees a wrong time, and it can be hours or days old.
findings.explanation: The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` once, when the module is imported. `from_integration` never passes `queued`, so every AssignmentSource built in a long-running worker or web process gets the same stale timestamp, which is the process start time. `to_dict()` then serializes that stale value into the task kwargs.
findings.title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at import time

findings.consequence: An authenticated request with a malformed backupCode returns a 500 where it should return a 400 IncorrectBackupCode.
findings.explanation: The handler calls req.body.backupCode.replaceAll without checking the type. If the JSON body sends a number, object or array as backupCode, replaceAll is not a function and the call throws a TypeError.
findings.title: Non-string backupCode causes an unhandled exception

findings.consequence: An attacker who knows only a victim's email can obtain a session for any account without 2FA by sending an arbitrary totpCode. This is a full authentication bypass. The new backupCode path also lets 2FA accounts be entered without their password.
findings.explanation: In authorize, the password is verified only when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` (lines 121-129). The identity-provider checks at lines 113-119 are also skipped when totpCode is present. Nothing later verifies the password. The 2FA block at lines 131-187 runs only when `user.twoFactorEnabled` is true. For a user with twoFactorEnabled=false, submitting the email and any non-empty totpCode (for example "1") passes every check, and the function returns the user at line 205. For a 2FA user, the new backup-code branch (131-156) adds another route. Submitting the email, any totpCode and a valid backupCode skips the password check, and only the backup code is verified. A non-CAL identity-provider account is also reachable this way.
findings.title: Password check skipped whenever totpCode is supplied, allowing login with only an email

findings.consequence: A single-use backup code can be replayed in parallel to create several sessions. A consumed code can also be restored by a racing write. This weakens the single-use guarantee of the second factor.
findings.explanation: The user row, including the encrypted backupCodes blob, is read at the start of authorize. The code decrypts the blob, finds the index, sets that slot to null in memory, then re-encrypts the whole array and writes it with prisma.user.update({where:{id}}). The update has no condition on the stored backupCodes value and there is no transaction or lock. Two concurrent requests with the same valid backup code both read the old blob, both find the code, and both succeed. The second write also overwrites the first. If two different codes are used concurrently, one write can restore the other code that was just consumed. The per-email rate limit does not prevent this, because both requests can arrive within the allowed count.
findings.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so one code can be used more than once

findings.consequence: Split-shift hosts lose valid slots in all but one of their ranges on the day. For non-fixed hosts and for hosts with seat-cached `selectedSlots`, this check now also removes those slots. Slots that overrun the end of working hours are still offered, because the end is never checked.
findings.explanation: In `checkIfIsAvailable`, `end` is computed from `slotStartTime` (`slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`), so it equals `start`. It should use the slot end time. The check `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore never looks at the slot's end, and a slot that starts before closing but runs past it is accepted. Separately, `workingHours.find` returns true, which rejects the slot, as soon as ANY entry for that weekday doesn't contain the slot. A host with a split shift (for example 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00 on the same day) has two entries for that day. A 14:00 slot is outside the first entry, so `find` returns true and the slot is marked unavailable, even though the second entry covers it. The same pattern appears in the date-override `find`. With two override ranges on one date, a slot inside the second range is before or after the first range and is rejected. In addition, `…
findings.title: Working-hours check in checkIfIsAvailable compares the slot start to itself and rejects slots in multi-range days

prs.title: Advanced date override handling and timezone compatibility improvements

findings.consequence: Non-SMS reminders with retryCount > 1 are deleted by the SMS cron and are never sent. This is data loss. It is latent if only the SMS path increments retryCount, but it is not enforced.
findings.explanation: The second OR branch of the deleteMany (lines 38-42) filters only on retryCount > 1 and has no method: SMS condition. It therefore matches WorkflowReminder rows of any method, such as EMAIL or WHATSAPP, whose retryCount exceeds 1. The previous query was restricted to SMS. The SMS cron should only remove its own reminders.
findings.title: retryCount cleanup deletes reminders of every method

findings.consequence: Today only the SMS path writes retryCount, so the impact is limited. If another reminder method starts using the column, this SMS endpoint will silently delete its reminders, including ones that are already scheduled.
findings.explanation: The new second OR branch in the deleteMany, `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`, has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` condition. The first branch is scoped to SMS. This is the SMS cron handler, and it only increments retryCount for SMS reminders. But the column is on the shared WorkflowReminder table, so the branch matches any reminder with retryCount > 1, whatever its method. Any email or WhatsApp reminder that later gets a retryCount above 1 would be deleted by this SMS cron endpoint.
findings.title: retryCount cleanup delete is not limited to SMS reminders

findings.consequence: One failing reminder, or a failing bookkeeping write, stops SMS scheduling for every later reminder in the batch on that cron run. Reminders with no message or recipient are re-processed on every run without being counted.
findings.explanation: The new retryCount update inside the catch block (lines 190-197) is not wrapped in its own try/catch. If it throws, for example on a DB error or a reminder row deleted concurrently (Prisma P2025), the exception escapes the for-loop and the handler. The remaining reminders are not processed and no response is sent normally. Separately, reminders with an empty message or missing sendTo skip both the schedule and the retryCount update (line 163 condition has no else). They are re-fetched on every cron run until scheduledDate passes, so the retry accounting is inconsistent.
findings.title: Unguarded prisma update in catch aborts the whole batch

prs.title: SMS workflow reminder retry count tracking

findings.consequence: Existing attendees and blacklisted addresses get unwanted or incorrect notification emails. Team admins who are not owners cannot add guests to team bookings.
findings.explanation: The handler filters `guests` into `uniqueGuests`. That filter removes emails that are already attendees and emails on the blacklist. Only `uniqueGuests` is saved as new attendees. The email step then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the unfiltered input. A concrete input: the booking already has attendee a@x.com, and the request is `guests: [a@x.com, b@x.com]`. Only b@x.com is added, but a@x.com is also sent a "guests added" email. A blacklisted address in `guests` also gets an email even though it was deliberately skipped. The send is wrapped in a try/catch that only logs, so nothing flags the mismatch. A second defect is in the permission check. `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)` uses `&&` where `||` is intended. Only a user who passes both checks counts as a team admin or owner. If `isTeamAdmin` includes owners, as I expect, team admins who are not owners are denied.…
findings.title: Add-guests emails are sent to the raw input list, not the filtered unique guests

findings.consequence: The number of stored devices can exceed device_limit under concurrent load.
findings.explanation: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in a separate statement. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all read count < limit and all insert.
findings.title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert

findings.consequence: With device_limit reached, any client that sends a device ID and retries is granted anonymous access. The limit only blocks the first attempt per device ID. Untracked devices can also be created without bound.
findings.explanation: Authenticate now rejects a request when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. In impl.go, tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before CreateOrUpdateDevice (impl.go:87 and :93). The cache entry therefore remains after the store rejects the device. A new device is refused on its first request. For the next 29 minutes, tagDeviceUI finds the key in the cache, returns nil, and Authenticate lets the same device ID through as anonymous. The device was never stored, so it is never counted against the limit.
findings.title: Device limit is bypassed on the second request because the rejected device stays in the local cache

findings.consequence: A device that is over the anonymous device limit is rejected on its first request. It then gets anonymous access on retry, although it was never stored, so the limit is effectively bypassed.
findings.explanation: The change makes TagDevice return the error from tagDeviceUI, so Anonymous.Authenticate rejects a request with ErrDeviceLimitReached. tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before CreateOrUpdateDevice and doesn't remove the key when the write fails. When the limit is hit, the first request from a new device is rejected. For the next 29 minutes, every request from that device finds the cache key, returns nil without touching the store, and authenticates as anonymous. The limit is therefore enforced only once per device.
findings.title: Propagated device-limit error is only returned once because the cache is set before the store write

findings.consequence: A user can be wrongly denied access to a resource they are allowed to see for the cache TTL, after a different resource with an ambiguous name/parent split was denied. This is a fail-closed error, not an authorization bypass.
findings.explanation: userPermDenialCacheKey builds its key as namespace.perm_uid_action_name_parent. Name and parent are request-controlled and can contain "_". Check(name="a_b", parent="c") and Check(name="a", parent="b_c") therefore produce the same key. A denial cached for one request makes Check return Allowed:false for the other without evaluating permissions. The key also shares the "<ns>.perm_<uid>_<action>" prefix with userPermCacheKey. I did not verify whether cacheWrap shares one keyspace across its caches. If it does, a name/parent that collides with the shape of a permission key could mix stored types.
findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous because it joins request-controlled fields with "_"
